One distinction matters: Secondary School Teachers, Except Special And Career/Technical Education explain established knowledge, while Environmental Science Teachers, Postsecondary must also produce research results. Publications, grants, and patents can all affect reviews.

This career does not suit people who want to teach without conducting research. Dedicated teaching positions are limited, and research carries heavy weight in university reviews. Teaching alone can weaken renewal prospects.

A common path is a bachelor's degree in environmental science or ecology, followed by a master's degree, doctorate, postdoctoral work, Lecturer, and Associate Professor. Independent colleges and vocational institutions offer more teaching-focused roles, but most universities assess both teaching and research.

This career suits people who enjoy teaching and can tolerate the slow, repetitive parts of research. People who can make complex ecological models clear to students and spend long hours resolving a data problem can thrive.

Environmental Science Teachers, Postsecondary teach environmental science, ecology, pollution control, and related subjects at universities and vocational colleges. They also conduct research, supervise undergraduate and graduate students, build academic programs, and provide public or industry service.

paragraphs: Teaching and research usually run in parallel. A teacher can lecture in the morning, supervise student data work in a laboratory in the afternoon, and write papers or revise grant proposals at night. Semesters also include thesis defenses, peer reviews, and conferences. Sampling seasons bring fieldwork, and deadlines can require sustained intensive work.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, about 9,000 Environmental Science Teachers, Postsecondary were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 9,300 by 2034, a net increase of about 300 jobs, with about 700 openings each year. The approximate median annual wage in 2026 is $87,700 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace Environmental Science Teachers, Postsecondary, but it will reshape the early stages of teaching and research. It increasingly handles slide drafts, literature reviews, grading, and data analysis, which consume much of a teacher's desk time. Teachers can invest the saved time in live instruction, laboratory guidance, research design, and industry service. Human judgment remains essential for making knowledge meaningful to students and guiding research toward results.

paragraphs: A score of 7/10 indicates moderate-high exposure because this career includes substantial desk work. Lesson planning, literature reviews, grading, and statistics are all well suited to AI.

Moderate-high exposure does not mean high risk. AI drives lesson-preparation costs down and makes teaching quality and research direction more visible. It pressures roles based on reading slides, while teachers who design project-based classes and guide research results enter performance reviews with stronger evidence.

Plan for a long path from bachelor's degree through master's degree, doctorate, and postdoctoral work. Build writing and data-analysis skills, join substantive research projects, and keep environmental-industry roles as an alternative instead of treating a university position as the only outcome.

Use AI as an assistant for lesson preparation and grading, then invest the saved time in laboratory guidance and research design. Adopt virtual simulation, remote-sensing instruction, and other new methods because teaching innovation strengthens performance reviews.

Environmental science doctorate holders should apply beyond universities. Environmental design institutes, consultancies, and corporate ESG teams also recruit them. Present teaching, research, and industry projects together instead of discussing publications alone.

Hiring and reviews should measure teaching outcomes, student feedback, and service results, not only publication counts. Give teachers AI lesson-planning and laboratory tools so they can focus on higher-value teaching and research.

Teachers also stay close to current research, making the career a strong fit for people who enjoy explaining ideas and investigating questions.

The greatest risk is not AI but university staffing and evaluation. Competition for faculty posts is intense, and up-or-out systems create heavy research pressure. Environmental science also depends strongly on environmental industries and policy, so sector demand directly affects enrollment and funding.
